Read .claude/hooks/api-route-discriminate-reminder.py in full. Grepped CLAUDE.md, _design-system/REMOVED.md and _docs/BACKEND.md for any frozen error-shape/pagination/naming law (none found beyond one line about computed-filter correctness). Ran my own sampling independent of the audit's numbers: grep -rhoE error-shape patterns across all app/api/**/route.ts (1579 x {error:..}, 251 x {message:..}, 47 x {success:..}), then hand-read the actual response bodies in 12 route files (salons, bookings, reviews, discovery favorites/toggle, dashboard/batch, auth/login, vouchers/create, health, loyalty, staff/[id], staff/invite, directory/[id]/claim) to classify distinct SHAPES rather than just count keywords. Ran grep -rl Cache-Control/revalidate across app/api (4 and 9 hits respectively). Ran grep for Location header on the 44 status:201 files (0 hits outside two unrelated redirect routes). Ran grep for MAX_BODY/sizeLimit/content-length across app/api and lib (0 hits). Ran grep for fetch("https://...") in app/api (8 call sites) then checked each individually for AbortController/AbortSignal.timeout (0 of 8 have one). Ran find for *.test.ts/*.spec.ts across the whole repo excluding node_modules/.next (8 total, all either money-logic unit tests under tests/lib or 2 Playwright visual specs; zero touch an API route's response shape). Listed app/api top-level directories to check naming grammar (found /api/salon singular + /api/salons plural coexisting, and nail/nail-discovery/nail-inspo/nail-tech as four separate top-level namespaces). Confirmed via ls that _backend-system/ has no LAW.md, RATIONALE.md, AUDIT_2026-07-16.md, or QUESTIONS.md on disk, only README.md plus the research/ and audit/ subfolders.

findings.title: No canonical error response shape, and nothing enforces the one recommended
findings.principle: Every API route that returns a client error responds with exactly one JSON shape: { error: { code: SCREAMING_SNAKE_STRING, message: string } }, status set on the HTTP status line, never duplicated as a body-only 'success' flag. No new or touched route.ts file may introduce a different top-level key set for an error body. A lint rule or PR-time grep check fails a route that returns any of the four other shapes already living in the codebase.
findings.why: A client (especially the mobile app, which lives in a separate repo and cannot read the web route source at build time) needs ONE parsing path for 'this call failed' to render a consistent error UI and to log a stable code for support triage. With five shapes coexisting, every new screen's fetch wrapper either special-cases per-endpoint or silently drops fields (a `.message` read against a `{error}`-only body is `undefined`).
findings.local_evidence: Hand-read 12 route files and found 5 distinct top-level error shapes in active use: {error,code} (app/api/staff/[id]/route.ts:13,22,26,29), {message,code} (app/api/bookings/route.ts:21,43,66,144; app/api/reviews/route.ts:18,28,44,45,46), {error} alone (app/api/dashboard/batch/route.ts:22,30,39; app/api/vouchers/create/route.ts:60; app/api/directory/[id]/claim/route.ts:42,46,66,70,87), {message} alone (app/api/auth/login/route.ts:44,54,65,69), and {error,message,code} combined (app/api/salons/route.ts:725: `{ error: "Failed to create salon", message: insertErr.message, code: "DB_ERROR" }`). The worst instance is that app/api/salons/route.ts itself mixes TWO shapes internally: line 628 returns {error,code} while line 651 returns {message,code}, in the same file, a few hundred lines apart.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rhoE '\{\s*(error|message|success|code)\s*:' app/api --include=route.ts | sort | uniq -c gave 1579 {error:, 251 {message:, 47 {success: with no single dominant convention; grep -rn 'error shape\|canonical error\|Problem Details' CLAUDE.md _design-system _rules _docs/BACKEND.md returned zero hits for any FROZEN rule (only the research file at _backend-system/research/api-design.md section 6 which recommends but does not enforce RFC 9457 adoption for new routes going forward); grep confirmed _backend-system/LAW.md does not exist on disk at all.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/api-design.md section 6 and _backend-system/audit/api-design.md row API-07 both correctly diagnose the {error,code}/{message,code} split (1356/223 occurrences project-wide by their count) and recommend adopting an RFC-9457-style shape for new/touched routes only, explicitly rejecting a mass migration as premature. What is missing is the DELTA this finding adds: (a) the research never picked a single concrete target shape, just 'RFC 9457 or a subset', so two engineers reading the research today would still converge on different shapes, and (b) there is zero mechanism, gate or otherwise, that would catch a new route introducing a SIXTH shape tomorrow.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (new file, does not exist yet) as the api-design section's first row, cross-referenced from CLAUDE.md's precedence chain the same way LOCKFILE.md is
findings.enforcement: gate: a lint rule (custom ESLint rule or a small grep-based pre-commit script, mirroring the existing solen-drift-check pattern) that flags any NextResponse.json(...) call in app/api with a 4xx/5xx status whose body's top-level keys are not exactly {error:{code,message}}

findings.title: No canonical success response envelope either
findings.principle: Every API route that returns a list wraps it as { items: T[], total: number, page: number, limit: number } (never a domain-named key like `bookings` in place of `items`); every route that returns a single created/fetched resource wraps it as { data: T }; every route that returns only a boolean outcome wraps it as { data: { ok: true } }, never a bespoke key like `saved`, `sent`, or a bare `{ ok: true }` at the top level.
findings.why: The same client-side unwrapping problem as the error shape: a generic `apiFetch<T>()` helper on either client (web or, more importantly, the separate-repo mobile app) can only exist if it can assume ONE place to find the payload. Right now every screen's data-fetching code has to know, per endpoint, whether the list is called `items` or `bookings`, whether a toggle result is `{saved}` or `{ok}`, which defeats the purpose of having a shared fetch wrapper at all and makes every new mobile screen a fresh reverse-engineering exercise against the web route's source.
findings.local_evidence: Hand-read the non-error NextResponse.json calls in 7 sampled files and found 7 distinct top-level success shapes: {items,total,page,limit} (app/api/salons/route.ts:141,211,451,614,625), {bookings,total,page,limit} AND {items,total,page,limit} in the SAME FILE for two different handlers (app/api/bookings/route.ts:86 vs :113), {data} (app/api/reviews/route.ts:149), {saved:boolean} (app/api/favorites/toggle/route.ts:76,88), {results} (app/api/dashboard/batch/route.ts:117), {ok:true} (app/api/staff/[id]/route.ts:54,82), and {sent:true,email:string} (app/api/directory/[id]/claim/route.ts:160).
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'success envelope\|response envelope\|canonical response shape' CLAUDE.md _design-system _backend-system _docs/BACKEND.md returned zero hits; _backend-system/research/api-design.md discusses error shape (section 6) and pagination style (section 4) but never once addresses the SUCCESS envelope as a distinct question, so this gap exists even inside the otherwise-thorough research file, not just in the frozen-law layer.
findings.existing_coverage: none: the research file's own section list (0-11) has no heading for 'success response shape'; it was not researched, audited, or recommended anywhere in the domain's existing prior art.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, api-design section, immediately after the error-shape row
findings.enforcement: gate: same lint/grep mechanism as api-contracts-01, checking the success-path top-level keys of any NextResponse.json in a route that also has a paginated .range() or .limit() call nearby (for the list-shape rule specifically)

findings.title: The project's own named #1 backend failure mode has only an informational reminder, never a blocking gate
findings.principle: Any route.ts file that reads a query-string filter parameter must ship with a discriminate-proof: either an automated test that calls the endpoint with and without the filter and asserts the result COUNTS differ, or a code comment linking to one, checked at PR/commit time, not merely surfaced as a post-edit reminder the author can read and ignore.
findings.why: A filter that renders in the UI, returns 200, and quietly returns the unfiltered set is indistinguishable from a working filter until a user notices the wrong salons showing up, exactly the failure class this project has already shipped once (the day-name key mismatch that made 'open now' return empty everywhere, per CLAUDE.md's own silent-no-op section). An informational hook that only injects a paragraph of text after the edit already happened relies entirely on the same session choosing to act on it; nothing stops the edit from being committed with the filter still broken.
findings.local_evidence: .claude/hooks/api-route-discriminate-reminder.py's own docstring states its exact scope at line 9: 'Informational, never blocks; once per file per session.' It fires PostToolUse (after the edit already landed), prints additionalContext, and exits 0 unconditionally (lines 42-58); there is no check anywhere in the hook that a test or proof was actually added, and it fires at most ONCE per file per session (line 33's marker file), so a second edit to the same file in the same session gets no reminder at all.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'discriminate' .claude/hooks/*.py returned only this one reminder-style hook, no PreToolUse or blocking counterpart; find . -iname '*.test.ts' -o -iname '*.spec.ts' (excluding node_modules/.next) returned 8 files total, none under app/api or testing any route's filter behavior, confirming no automated discriminate-proof exists for any filter in the codebase today.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the hook exists and correctly names the exact failure mode and the exact three-part proof procedure (filter discrimination, live-column existence, computed-filter ordering before .range()); the missing delta is entirely about ENFORCEMENT TIMING AND FORCE, advisory-after-the-fact versus a gate that can actually block a commit or PR.
findings.where_it_should_live: either upgrade .claude/hooks/api-route-discriminate-reminder.py itself to a PreToolUse blocking check when it can detect a searchParams.get(...) used directly in a .eq()/.gte()/.contains() filter with no adjacent test file, or add a lightweight CI check (pre-commit-graveyard.sh already exists as a precedent for a blocking git hook in this repo) that requires a matching test file for any route touching a new filter param

findings.title: Zero automated contract tests exist for any API route's shape, status code, or pagination behavior
findings.principle: Every route.ts under app/api that is customer-facing (not admin/cron/dev-only) ships at least one integration test asserting: the success shape matches the canonical envelope (api-contracts-02), the error shape matches the canonical error contract (api-contracts-01), and a documented status code is returned for each documented failure branch. A route with zero mutating handlers (a pure read with no filters) is exempt.
findings.why: Even once a canonical shape is written down (findings 1 and 2), nothing catches a future edit that quietly reverts to an old shape, mixes in a new one, or changes a status code, unless a human happens to notice in review. Contract drift is invisible until a client (especially the separate-repo mobile app, which cannot see the web route's source diff) breaks in production.
findings.local_evidence: find . -iname '*.test.ts' -o -iname '*.spec.ts' across the whole repo (excluding node_modules and .next) returns exactly 8 files: 6 unit tests under tests/lib/{bookings,purchases} testing pure money-calculation functions (issue-refund, off-session-charge, charge-fee, customer-cancel-money, dispute-engine) plus 2 Playwright visual specs under e2e/visual (spine.spec.ts, homepage.spec.ts). None of the 357 files under app/api/**/route.ts has a corresponding test file anywhere in the repo.
findings.absence_proof: find . -path ./node_modules -prune -o -path ./.next -prune -o \( -iname '*.test.ts' -o -iname '*.spec.ts' \) -print gave 8 results total, zero matching 'api' or 'route' in path or content; grep -rn 'contract test\|api test\|supertest\|route handler test' package.json CLAUDE.md _backend-system returned zero hits for any tooling or convention around API-route testing.
findings.existing_coverage: none: neither the research file nor the audit file mentions contract/integration testing as a topic at all; this is a genuinely uncovered sub-area of the domain's own scope (the orchestrator's brief lists 'contract tests' explicitly as in-scope).
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (a new 'testing' row under api-design) plus a concrete starter: a tests/api/ directory with one supertest-or-fetch-based smoke test per customer-facing route group (salons, bookings, reviews) as the first slice, not a demand to backfill all 357 at once (scale-appropriate: with 28 salons and one small team, backfilling 357 route tests today is disproportionate; the trigger to expand coverage further is the first production incident traced to an undetected contract change, or the mobile app's release cadence outpacing the web team's ability to manually verify shared-endpoint changes)

findings.title: Zero of the sampled 201-Created responses set a Location header, confirming the research's own open question
findings.principle: Every 201 Created response sets a Location header pointing at the created resource's canonical GET URL (e.g. `/api/bookings/{id}`), even when the same data is also echoed in the body. A route that creates a resource with no addressable GET-by-id endpoint yet must either add one or explicitly note in a code comment why Location is omitted.
findings.why: RFC 9110 section 15.3.2 pairs 201 with the expectation that the client can locate the new resource; a client that wants to re-fetch, deep-link, or share a reference to the thing it just created has to fall back to guessing a URL shape from the body's id field, which only works if every client independently knows the same URL-construction convention, exactly the kind of implicit coupling a Location header exists to remove.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rn 'status: 201' app/api --include=route.ts returns 44 matches; grep -rl 'Location' app/api --include=route.ts returns only 4 files, and reading all 4 (app/api/auth/callback/route.ts, app/api/transit/nearest-stop/route.ts, app/api/recommendations/route.ts, app/api/dev/login/route.ts) shows every occurrence is either a code comment mentioning OAuth redirect Location, a geo-location variable name, or a 307 redirect's Location header, none of them a 201-Created response's Location header. Zero of the 44 status:201 responses (sample included app/api/nail-discovery/publish/route.ts:73, app/api/clients/[id]/intake/route.ts:86, app/api/clients/[id]/photos/route.ts:101, app/api/clients/[id]/nail-history/route.ts:104, app/api/clients/[id]/formulas/route.ts:77) sets one.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'Location' app/api --include=route.ts | grep -v 'redirect\|OAuth\|geo\|307' returns zero hits tied to any 201 response.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/api-design.md's own 'Unverified' section (line 252 area) explicitly flags this exact question as unchecked ('Whether every one of Solen's 45 existing 201 responses actually sets a Location header; this was not checked file-by-file'). This finding closes that open question with a direct measurement: the answer is zero, not 'some do, some don't', which raises it from an open question to a confirmed, name-worthy gap the research itself predicted might exist.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, api-design section, as a concrete row (currently only a bulleted recommendation in the research prose, section 0 item 2)
findings.enforcement: gate: the same status-code lint rule as api-contracts-01/02 can check that any NextResponse.json(..., {status:201}) call sets a headers.Location entry

findings.title: Every outbound third-party fetch() call inside an API route has zero timeout, independent of the AI-generation case already flagged
findings.principle: Any fetch() call to a third-party HTTP endpoint inside a route.ts file passes an explicit AbortSignal.timeout(N) (N chosen per call: a few seconds for a fast lookup like a transit-station query, longer for a genuinely slow provider), so a hung third-party service fails the request in a controlled, fast, named way instead of consuming the serverless function's entire wall-clock budget and returning the platform's generic timeout error.
findings.why: A route handler running on a serverless function has a hard wall-clock ceiling; a fetch with no timeout can hold that budget hostage until the PLATFORM kills it, at which point the caller gets an opaque 502/504 with none of Solen's own error-shape or logging discipline attached, and any other work the handler still had to do (writing a DB row, sending a notification) never happens either.
findings.local_evidence: grep for outbound fetch("https://...") calls in app/api found exactly 8 call sites: app/api/bookings/resend-access/route.ts, app/api/bookings/[id]/dispute/route.ts, app/api/bookings/[id]/report/route.ts, app/api/bookings/[id]/escalate/route.ts, app/api/auth/verify-phone/send/route.ts, app/api/admin/nail/generate/route.ts, app/api/loyalty/award/route.ts, app/api/dashboard/barber-reminders/send/route.ts. Checking each individually for AbortController or AbortSignal.timeout: 0 of 8 have one.
findings.absence_proof: for f in $(grep -rl 'fetch("https://\|fetch(`https://' app/api --include=route.ts); do grep -q 'AbortController\|AbortSignal.timeout' "$f" || echo "NO-TIMEOUT: $f"; done printed all 8 files with no match found in any.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/api-design.md section 9 and the audit's API-10 row both correctly flag the SAME underlying platform risk (Netlify function wall-clock limits) but scope it narrowly to AI-generation routes needing a 202+poll architecture. The delta this finding adds: four of the eight zero-timeout call sites (resend-access, dispute, report, escalate, barber-reminders) have nothing to do with AI generation or long-running jobs, they are simple notification/SMS/webhook-style outbound calls that should be FAST and don't need job/poll infrastructure at all, they just need a timeout guard, a much cheaper and more general fix than the 202+poll architecture the existing research scoped this problem to.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, api-design or reliability section, as its own row distinct from the long-running-operations row (which stays about the 202+poll architecture question)
findings.enforcement: gate: a grep-based pre-commit check (same family as pre-commit-graveyard.sh) that flags a new fetch("https://...") call in app/api with no AbortSignal/AbortController in the same function body

findings.title: No resource-naming grammar is written down anywhere, and the surface already shows drift
findings.principle: A route segment name is singular only when it addresses a resource scoped to the authenticated caller's own single instance of it (e.g. `/api/salon/*` for 'my own salon's sub-resources'); it is plural for any public or admin-facing collection (e.g. `/api/salons`). A new top-level namespace for an existing domain (nail, discovery, inspo, tech) requires either extending an existing namespace or a one-line note in the route file explaining why a new one was needed instead.
findings.why: With 357 routes across dozens of top-level namespaces, an unwritten naming convention decays into ad hoc choices per feature, making it harder for a new session (or a new engineer) to guess where a given capability lives without grepping, and increasing the odds of literally duplicating a namespace (a `/api/nail-tech` next to `/api/nail`, `/api/nail-discovery`, `/api/nail-inspo` already existing) rather than extending one.
findings.local_evidence: ls app/api shows both `salon` (singular, containing stations/clients/invoices/last-minute-settings/go-live/retail/loyalty/dynamic-pricing/chairs/earnings/documents/closures/services/bundles/setup-progress, all owner-scoped-to-caller sub-resources) and `salons` (plural, the public search/list/detail collection) coexisting with no written rule distinguishing the two conventions. Separately, the nail domain is split across FOUR top-level namespaces: `nail` (hand-chart, retail, pricing), `nail-discovery` (publish), `nail-inspo` (images, boards), and `nail-tech` ([id]), with no doc stating the boundary between them.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rni 'route naming\|resource naming\|naming convention\|singular.*plural\|kebab-case' _docs/BACKEND.md _backend-system _rules CLAUDE.md returned zero hits for any written naming grammar; the only 'naming convention' hits found anywhere in the codebase's docs are about OpenTelemetry semantic conventions (observability research, unrelated) and Google AIP batch-method naming (a different sub-topic already covered).
findings.existing_coverage: none: resource/route naming grammar is explicitly listed in this domain's scope by the orchestrator's brief but is not addressed anywhere in the existing research or audit files, nor in CLAUDE.md or _docs/BACKEND.md.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, a new short row under api-design; low cost to write since it mostly needs to CODIFY the singular/plural distinction that already exists in practice for salon/salons, then extend it as a rule for future namespace decisions
findings.enforcement: checklist: a one-line addition to whatever pre-route-creation exists-check protocol is already run (the project's own `npm run exists <keyword>` convention already fires before any new route; add a naming-grammar reminder to that same check's output rather than building new tooling)

findings.title: No request-body size limit exists anywhere in the API surface
findings.principle: Any route handler that calls request.json() on a body that could plausibly grow large (an array-accepting batch endpoint, a text/description field, a base64-encoded upload) enforces an explicit maximum, either via a zod .max()/.length() constraint on the parsed shape or a raw byte-length check on the request before parsing; the default assumption for a NEW route is a body under a few KB unless a documented reason requires more.
findings.why: Next.js App Router Route Handlers, unlike the old Pages API's bodyParser, impose no default size limit on `request.json()`; the only backstop today is whatever ceiling the hosting platform enforces on the whole request, not anything Solen's own code chooses or can reason about per endpoint. An endpoint with no size discipline is a resource-exhaustion vector: a single request with an oversized array or string can consume disproportionate memory/CPU parsing it before any business-logic validation even runs, on a serverless function billed and rate-limited per invocation.
findings.local_evidence: The dashboard/batch endpoint already named in api-contracts-09's sibling finding (audit row API-09) is a concrete live example: app/api/dashboard/batch/route.ts:27-31 casts the parsed body's `requests` field directly to `BatchKey[]` with only an `Array.isArray` check, no length cap, before fanning it out into a `Promise.all` of Supabase queries.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'MAX_BODY\|content-length\|maxBodyLength\|bodySize\|sizeLimit' app/api lib --include='*.ts' returned zero hits across the entire route and lib surface; grep -n 'bodySizeLimit\|serverActions' next.config.js/mjs/ts returned zero hits, confirming Next's own experimental serverActions.bodySizeLimit config (which only applies to Server Actions, not Route Handlers, anyway) is not in use either.
findings.existing_coverage: none: request/response size limits are explicitly in this domain's scope per the orchestrator's brief but are not mentioned anywhere in the research or audit files; the audit's API-09 row flags the SAME dashboard/batch endpoint for a missing array-length cap but frames it purely as a batch-operation-contract gap (atomic-vs-partial-success), not as an instance of a missing general size-limit principle.
findings.enforcement: checklist item folded into the existing zod-at-the-boundary discipline (already 69% adopted per the audit's API-08 row): every new zod schema for a mutating route must include an explicit .max() on any array or free-text field, not leave it open-ended

findings.title: No stated policy for which endpoints should set Cache-Control, so caching is each author's ad hoc, undocumented call
findings.principle: A route handler explicitly sets one of exactly two cache policies: `Cache-Control: private, no-store` for anything reading or returning user-specific, payment, or auth-adjacent data (the safe default for a new route), or a documented public/anonymous cache policy (max-age + stale-while-revalidate, matching the existing `ANON_CACHE_HEADERS` pattern) for genuinely public, non-personalized data like the salon search/list endpoints. No route ships with neither set.
findings.why: Deliberate caching is a real, already-used pattern (lib/salons/cache-headers.ts's `ANON_CACHE_HEADERS`) but it's applied to only 4 of 357 route files today with no written rule for when a NEW route should reach for it, and more importantly no explicit no-store default stated for the routes that must NEVER be cached. If a CDN or edge cache is ever added in front of Netlify (a plausible future performance step), an endpoint that happens to look cacheable by a generic heuristic (a GET with no obvious auth header) but actually returns per-user or payment-status data would silently leak across users unless every such route already declares its own explicit no-store today.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rl 'Cache-Control' app/api returns exactly 4 files (app/api/salon-of-month/route.ts, app/api/discovery/thumb/[id]/route.ts, app/api/discovery/category-meta/route.ts, app/api/loyalty/qr/[cardId]/route.ts); grep -rl 'revalidate' app/api returns 9 files. Of the 357 total route files, roughly 344 (357 minus the 4 with Cache-Control minus other revalidate-only hits) set no caching header at all, relying entirely on Next.js/Netlify's own defaults for a Route Handler, which are dynamic-by-default but not something the codebase asserts or tests.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'cache policy\|Cache-Control policy\|no-store default' CLAUDE.md _backend-system _docs/BACKEND.md returned zero hits for any written rule distinguishing which routes should or shouldn't cache.
findings.existing_coverage: none: caching is listed as one of the 15 topics in _backend-system's own topic list (`caching`) and has its own dedicated research file (_backend-system/research/caching.md, not read in depth for this pass since it's a sibling domain), but the API-CONTRACT-SPECIFIC question of 'which route categories get which Cache-Control value, stated as a rule new route authors can follow without reading the caching research file' is not addressed in the api-design research file itself, and no LAW.md row exists to connect the two domains.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, cross-referenced between the api-design and caching sections
findings.enforcement: doc-only for now given scale (28 salons, no CDN edge cache in front of Netlify today); becomes a real gate the day a CDN/edge cache is introduced in front of the API, at which point every route lacking an explicit Cache-Control must be treated as a blocking finding, not a style note

findings.title: The whole api-design domain's decisions exist only as unfrozen prose; no LAW.md row means every future session re-derives or contradicts them from scratch
findings.principle: Every decision this domain's research file already reached a clear recommendation on (REST-only, no versioning, deterministic idempotency keys on money paths, 422-for-business-rules going forward, keyset-vs-offset trigger at ~10k-50k rows, no OpenAPI today, no Sunset-header machinery today) gets copied as a one-line locked row into _backend-system/LAW.md, the file the folder's own README says is the actual answer a new session should read, but which does not exist on disk.
findings.why: The whole reason this backend law layer was commissioned (per _backend-system/README.md line 5, the owner's own words: 'it keeps making stuff up when I open a new session') is defeated if the frozen answer file never gets written. A 278-line research file with 15 sourced references is excellent INPUT to a decision but is not itself the decision; a fresh session under time pressure is exactly as likely to re-litigate 'should we version the API' by skimming the research's nuanced tradeoff prose as it was to invent an answer from training memory before the research existed, because there is no single short row it can trust as already-settled.
findings.local_evidence: ls _backend-system/*.md shows only README.md at the folder root; _backend-system/LAW.md, _backend-system/RATIONALE.md, _backend-system/AUDIT_2026-07-16.md, and _backend-system/QUESTIONS.md, all four files the README's own layer map (lines 9-19) promises exist, are absent. Only research/api-design.md and audit/api-design.md (the per-topic files) exist for this domain.
findings.absence_proof: ls -la _backend-system/ confirms only README.md, research/, and audit/ are present at the folder root; find _backend-system -maxdepth 1 -iname 'LAW.md' -o -iname 'RATIONALE.md' -o -iname 'AUDIT_2026-07-16.md' -o -iname 'QUESTIONS.md' returns zero files.
findings.existing_coverage: none by definition: this is the meta-gap that makes every other finding in this file harder to act on, since there is nowhere to put a locked row today; each of findings 01-09 names _backend-system/LAW.md as its target location, and none of them can actually land until this finding is addressed first.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md itself (the file needs to be created, not edited)
findings.enforcement: gate: none exists or is proposed here since creating the missing file is a one-time authoring task, not an ongoing behavioral rule; the appropriate follow-up is a single dedicated pass (per topic, or all 15 at once) that converts each research file's 'Recommended default' lines into LAW.md rows, the same way _design-system/LOCKFILE.md was distilled from _design-system/SOURCE.md
